not_recommended.reason: The guideline considers either interdisciplinary or multidisciplinary care much better suited to the multifactorial presentation of CRPS.

not_recommended.name: Fixed progression through each rehabilitation level in 2 weeks or less
not_recommended.reason: The earlier Malibu time requirement is considered excessively rigid and unrealistic.

response_assessment.method: Assess functional use, range of motion, edema, pain, sensory changes, and progress toward individual activity goals.
response_assessment.interpretation: Lack of reasonable progress prompts adjustment of rehabilitation and consideration of concurrent interventions.

supportive_care: Address edema to facilitate range of motion.
Encourage general aerobic activity throughout rehabilitation.
Assess and actively treat secondary muscle spasm, guarding, disuse, and myofascial pain.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Interdisciplinary treatment is the preferred organizational approach, but the guideline notes that CRPS-specific high-quality evidence for the complete interdisciplinary program remains insufficient.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients beginning affected-limb reactivation, including those with sensory disturbance, edema, or movement avoidance.
decision_rules: Start with gentle, tolerable activities and increase sensory input and loading progressively.
Keep exercise within the patient's tolerance; both excessive activity and prolonged inactivity can worsen symptoms.
Do not perform physical therapy while the limb is insensate, including immediately after a block.

recommended_regimens.name: Desensitization
recommended_regimens.summary: Gradually expose the affected area to sensory stimulation alongside increasing functional use.

recommended_regimens.name: Edema management
recommended_regimens.summary: Use appropriate garments and manual edema mobilization while progressing movement and limb use.

recommended_regimens.name: Stress loading
recommended_regimens.summary: Introduce scrubbing and carrying to load affected joints; progressively increase load and activity time while encouraging use of the limb during daily tasks.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline describes clinical utility but states that comparative efficacy against other functional loading approaches requires study.

recommended_regimens.name: Gentle progressive exercise
recommended_regimens.summary: Progress active movement, flexibility, posture, gait, coordination, and strengthening as tolerated, incorporating pacing, breaks, and relaxation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Trials by Oerlemans et al. found better pain ratings and active mobility with physical therapy than with counseling alone in upper-extremity CRPS.

alternative_regimens.name: Aquatic therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Use buoyancy and water resistance to introduce movement and, particularly for the lower limb, weight bearing; avoid water temperatures that exacerbate symptoms.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be especially useful when early land-based loading is difficult.

alternative_regimens.name: Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation (PNF)
alternative_regimens.summary: Use movement patterns to develop strength, balance, and performance of daily activities.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be incorporated as functional movement becomes more tolerable.

alternative_regimens.name: Feldenkrais
alternative_regimens.summary: Use gentle active mat-based movement to develop body awareness and appropriate movement patterns.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An option for non-weight-bearing movement practice.

not_recommended.name: Inappropriately aggressive physical therapy
not_recommended.reason: It can provoke severe pain, edema, distress, and fatigue and may worsen inflammatory and sympathetic features.

not_recommended.name: Physical therapy while the affected limb is insensate
not_recommended.reason: The guideline says therapy should never be undertaken under this condition.

not_recommended.name: Prolonged ice application and inactivity
not_recommended.reason: Both may aggravate CRPS.

response_assessment.method: Monitor tolerance, edema, pain, range of motion, movement quality, and everyday limb use.
response_assessment.interpretation: Increase or reduce activity according to therapeutic response while continuing gradual functional progression.

supportive_care: Teach pacing and incorporate rest breaks.
Maintain normal posture and movement where possible to limit secondary compensatory problems.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Patients with CRPS-Type II and pronounced hypoesthesia require particular avoidance of exercise when the affected limb is insensate.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for early sensorimotor rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Individualize mirror-based or imagery treatment according to symptoms and observed response.
Do not continue these approaches if the patient cannot establish ownership of the mirrored limb or develops increased pain or movement disorder symptoms.
Recognize that results for graded motor imagery conflict and definitive clinical value is not established.

recommended_regimens.name: Mirror Visual Feedback
recommended_regimens.summary: Begin with descriptions and imagined movement of both limbs, then view the unaffected limb's reflection without movement before progressing according to response.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: McCabe et al. reported benefit in early and intermediate CRPS but no significant effect in chronic CRPS.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Home sessions of no more than 5 minutes, 5–6 times throughout the day.

alternative_regimens.name: Graded Motor Imagery
alternative_regimens.summary: Sequence limb laterality recognition, imagined movement, and mirror therapy. An initial small randomized trial reported greater pain improvement than standard treatment, but later studies did not reproduce improvement and one suggested increased pain and edema.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be integrated into an individualized rehabilitation program with close attention to symptom response.

alternative_regimens.name: Sensorimotor retuning
alternative_regimens.summary: Combine sensory retraining or desensitization with movement tasks; small preliminary studies reported reduced pain and improved sensory or proprioceptive measures.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A rehabilitation option supported by preliminary rather than definitive evidence.

response_assessment.method: Assess limb ownership, pain, edema, movement disorders, and ability to progress with functional movement.
response_assessment.interpretation: Increased pain, worsening movement disorder symptoms, or inability to establish mirror-limb ownership are contraindications identified by the cited protocols.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline describes both Mirror Visual Feedback and Graded Motor Imagery as patient-centered techniques whose ultimate value still requires definitive trials.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with pain-related fear, avoidance of movement, distress, or barriers to active rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Provide patients and families early education about disuse, reactivation, self-management, and possible interactions between distress and symptoms.
For persistent CRPS or inadequate response to limited intervention, perform individualized psychological assessment and offer targeted pain-management treatment.
Coordinate behavioral reactivation with functional therapists, balancing avoidance of disuse against severe pain exacerbations.

recommended_regimens.name: Patient and family education
recommended_regimens.summary: Explain the role of graded reactivation and active self-management to patients with acute or chronic CRPS and their families.

recommended_regimens.name: Psychological pain management
recommended_regimens.summary: Combine appropriate relaxation or mindfulness methods, cognitive pain-coping work, and behavioral management of avoidance; address family responses, major stressors, or psychiatric disorders when present.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The guideline considers CRPS-specific controlled evidence limited; studies of combined treatment suggest psychological care can contribute to comprehensive rehabilitation.

alternative_regimens.name: Graded exposure therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Target feared activities and learned movement avoidance through supported exposure. A randomized trial found greater improvements in pain, catastrophizing, perceived harmfulness of activity, and disability than with pain-contingent usual care at 6 month follow-up; another trial's per-protocol, but not intent-to-treat, analysis was consistent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Especially relevant when fear of movement obstructs reactivation.

alternative_regimens.name: ACT
alternative_regimens.summary: Support engagement in valued activities despite ongoing pain or discomfort.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: May be included in psychological pain management.

alternative_regimens.name: Relaxation training with biofeedback
alternative_regimens.summary: Teach relaxation, preferably with thermal and/or electromyographic biofeedback, and encourage regular practice during everyday activities.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Technique selection can reflect patient and therapist preference; no relaxation method has established superiority.

not_recommended.name: Psychological treatment alone as the complete treatment of CRPS
not_recommended.reason: The guideline says treatment confined to psychological aspects cannot adequately address the syndrome.

response_assessment.timepoint: At psychological evaluation and throughout treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess psychiatric comorbidity, emotional and behavioral responses, pain-related fear, beliefs about CRPS, ongoing stressors, family responses, and participation in reactivation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use identified barriers to select targeted interventions and adjust activity goals with the rehabilitation team.

supportive_care: Guide family members toward responses that support appropriate activity rather than reinforcing avoidance.
Treat identified psychiatric disorders as part of comprehensive care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline does not establish psychological factors as a necessary cause of CRPS; psychological care addresses potentially modifiable consequences and barriers to rehabilitation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients unable to start or advance functional restoration because of pain, allodynia, kinesiophobia, or substantial concomitant psychological symptoms.
decision_rules: Use additional treatment to create an opportunity for active rehabilitation rather than replacing functional restoration.
For mild to moderate pain, consider simple analgesics and/or blocks; for excruciating, intractable pain, the consensus guide lists opioids and/or blocks, with more experimental interventions later.
For significant allodynia or hyperalgesia, the consensus guide lists anticonvulsants, sodium channel blockers, or NMDA-receptor antagonists.
For depression, anxiety, or insomnia, consider relevant antidepressant or anxiolytic treatment and/or psychotherapy.

alternative_regimens.name: Sympathetic and/or somatic block
alternative_regimens.summary: May temporarily reduce severe allodynic pain enough to permit more active rehabilitation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Pain prevents initiation or advancement of functional treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Cognitive behavioral techniques
alternative_regimens.summary: Address fear that movement will inevitably cause harm.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Kinesiophobia obstructs rehabilitation.

alternative_regimens.name: Medication
alternative_regimens.summary: Select treatment according to the problem preventing progress, while continuing functional restoration.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Use when symptoms block progression or when significant concomitant problems warrant treatment from the outset.

not_recommended.name: Deferring all medication, blocks, and psychological support until rehabilitation failure
not_recommended.reason: The guideline notes that substantial presenting problems can require these interventions immediately.

response_assessment.method: Reassess comfort, ability to participate, and advancement in functional restoration.
response_assessment.interpretation: The intended benefit is progression to the next functional level.

supportive_care: Continue coordinated rehabilitation while addressing pain or psychological barriers.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The symptom-based pharmacotherapy guide is empirical and consensus-based; individual presentation takes precedence over its general suggestions.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients needing medication to manage symptoms and participate in rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Agree on realistic pain and functional targets with the patient before beginning a drug.
Prefer monotherapy where feasible, but use rational combinations from different drug classes when multiple symptoms require treatment.
Trial new drugs individually, increase methodically as appropriate, and discontinue treatment if benefit is unclear or adverse effects are intolerable.
Reconsider medication when agreed targets are not met or initial benefit wanes; weigh cost and individual needs.

alternative_regimens.name: Empirical pharmacotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Choose a drug according to the patient's presentation, the limited CRPS-specific evidence, and evidence from related pain conditions, alongside functional restoration.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptoms require additional control or obstruct rehabilitation.

not_recommended.name: Multiple medications from the same class without a rational basis
not_recommended.reason: The guideline favors monotherapy when possible and rational combinations across classes when polypharmacy is necessary.

not_recommended.name: Continuing an ineffective or intolerable drug
not_recommended.reason: The guideline calls for discontinuation when a methodical trial is not clearly helpful or adverse effects cannot be tolerated.

response_assessment.method: Agree on pain and activity targets, such as a pain reduction of two points on a 0–10 scale or improvement in specified activities, then compare subsequent response with those targets.
response_assessment.interpretation: Failure to meet targets or loss of earlier benefit calls for reconsidering the drug.

supportive_care: Continue functional restoration and address comorbid conditions.
Discuss that available drugs are not considered a cure and do not relieve symptoms in every patient.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Early CRPS may improve naturally, whereas persistent disease may respond differently. The guideline notes that analgesic tolerance can develop while adverse effects continue.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with early CRPS and prominent inflammation.
decision_rules: A short steroid course may be considered when inflammation is prominent early in the disease.
Do not assume that early improvement establishes drug efficacy, because spontaneous recovery can occur.

alternative_regimens.name: Steroids
alternative_regimens.summary: A short course may be indicated early after trauma when inflammatory features are prominent. The supportive studies have limitations, including one trial judged low quality by a systematic review.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Early CRPS with prominent inflammation.

alternative_regimens.name: NSAIDs
alternative_regimens.summary: Clinical experience suggests benefit for some patients, including potentially for associated proximal myofascial or muscle pain, but CRPS-specific research support is lacking and one study showed no analgesic value.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider according to inflammatory symptoms or accompanying muscle pain.

not_recommended.name: Chronic steroid treatment
not_recommended.reason: Longer courses have unproven benefit and chronic use has numerous serious contraindications.

not_recommended.name: acetaminophen for chronic disease
not_recommended.reason: The guideline does not currently recommend it because regular or high-dose use may cause liver toxicity.

response_assessment.method: Assess inflammation, pain, rehabilitation participation, and adverse effects.
response_assessment.interpretation: Consider whether benefit warrants continued treatment within the intended short course.

supportive_care: Continue functional rehabilitation and edema management.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The early post-trauma steroid evidence describes approximately 30mg/day for 2–12 weeks, followed by a taper; the guideline frames use as a possibility rather than an established treatment for all early CRPS.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with persistent CRPS being considered for immune-directed treatment.
decision_rules: Interpret preliminary responses alongside subsequent negative or unconfirmed trials.
Avoid treating experimental immune strategies as established options.

alternative_regimens.name: mycophenolate
alternative_regimens.summary: A small open-label randomized trial suggested efficacy at 1.5g BID, but confirmation in a larger trial is needed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The guideline presents it as preliminary evidence, not an established preferred regimen.

alternative_regimens.name: Plasma exchange
alternative_regimens.summary: Case series and clinical experience describe pain improvement in some cases, but repeated exchanges may be required and venous-access pain can complicate treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An incompletely established option in selected persistent cases.

not_recommended.name: Intrathecal steroid injection
not_recommended.reason: A single injection was shown ineffective.

not_recommended.name: infliximab
not_recommended.reason: A preliminary trial stopped early found it ineffective.

not_recommended.name: lenalidomide
not_recommended.reason: A large randomized trial in persistent CRPS found it ineffective.

supportive_care: Maintain rehabilitation-focused, patient-centered care while assessing treatment burden and adverse effects.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Intermediate-dose steroids totaling 1 g orally over 2weeks are rarely effective in persistent CRPS and often cause adverse effects. An initial low-dose IVIG trial suggested benefit, but a larger subsequent trial was negative. High-dose IVIG has not been formally tested; the guideline also describes other immune-directed approaches as requiring definitive trials.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients for whom neuropathic-pain medication is considered to support symptom control and rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Select treatment according to the individual's symptom pattern and tolerability rather than assuming evidence from other neuropathic conditions proves efficacy in CRPS.
If using tricyclic/heterocyclic drugs, begin at a low dose, increase gradually, and monitor closely; a low-dose trial alone is insufficient to conclude ineffectiveness.

recommended_regimens.name: Tricyclic/heterocyclic antidepressants
recommended_regimens.summary: The guideline regards these as particularly useful individual agents for CRPS symptoms, while drawing much of their efficacy evidence from other neuropathic pain conditions. Select among them according to accompanying anxiety, depression, insomnia, and adverse-effect profile.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: A cited neuropathic-pain study reported that, for every 100 patients taking antidepressants, 30 obtained at least 50% pain relief, with an NNT of 3; these are not CRPS-specific outcomes.

alternative_regimens.name: gabapentin
alternative_regimens.summary: Case reports suggested possible CRPS benefit, but the CRPS randomized trial was negative and used 1800mg/day, described as a sub-maximal dose.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An empirical option informed partly by evidence in other neuropathic pain conditions.

alternative_regimens.name: pregabalin
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline notes similarity to gabapentin and the possibility of twice-daily dosing for some patients, but identifies no CRPS clinical trial data.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider individual dosing needs and relative cost; CRPS efficacy is not established.

alternative_regimens.name: carbamazepine
alternative_regimens.summary: A preliminary randomized study in a selected group suggested some analgesic effect with 600 mg/day over 8 days.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The reported CRPS evidence is preliminary and arose in patients responsive to spinal cord stimulation.

alternative_regimens.name: doxepin
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline gives it as an example of a sedating antidepressant that might suit an anxious, depressed patient with insomnia.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to the patient's coexisting symptoms.

alternative_regimens.name: desipramine
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline gives it as an example of a more activating antidepressant for a patient with hypersomnolence and psychomotor retardation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Choose according to the patient's coexisting symptoms.

not_recommended.name: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) as analgesics
not_recommended.reason: The guideline states that they have not shown analgesic efficacy, although they may treat anxiety or depression.

response_assessment.timepoint: At initiation and during dose escalation
response_assessment.method: Monitor clinical benefit and expected adverse effects through frequent visits; obtain an EKG before reaching the mid-dose range and again at the ultimate tricyclic dose.
response_assessment.interpretation: Reassess the regimen if benefit is inadequate after an appropriate trial or tolerability is poor.

supportive_care: Continue functional restoration.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline reports no CRPS trials for oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, milnacipran, or duloxetine; anecdotal evidence alone is described for several other anticonvulsants and for venlafaxine.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with pain insufficiently managed by lower-risk treatment.
decision_rules: Consider an opioid trial at lower doses only after weighing alternatives; do not escalate freely when analgesia is inadequate.
Continuously reassess benefits against toxicity, tolerance, and possible worsening of hyperalgesia.

alternative_regimens.name: Opioids
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline describes lower-dose opioids as a reasonable 2nd or 3rd line option to try, with continuing assessment of risk and benefit. Its sole cited CRPS trial of controlled-release morphine found no pain-reduction difference from placebo after 8 days’ use, but is considered inadequate to settle short-term efficacy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients after consideration of less risky approaches.

not_recommended.name: Unrestricted opioid dose escalation
not_recommended.reason: Escalation can add adverse effects without additional relief; long-term high-dose use may worsen allodynia or hyperpathia.

response_assessment.method: Review analgesia, function, dose, adverse effects, tolerance, and signs of worsening pain sensitivity.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continue only with an acceptable balance of benefit and risk.

supportive_care: Continue active rehabilitation and other indicated non-opioid care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The cited overdose-risk study found that patients prescribed 100 mg or more of morphine or equivalent had a 9 times greater serious-overdose risk than those prescribed less than 20mg of morphine or equivalent daily. Frequent use of short-acting rescue opioids can effectively increase the daily dose and promote tolerance.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for NMDA receptor antagonist treatment because symptoms remain difficult to manage.
decision_rules: Distinguish evidence for sub-anesthetic intravenous ketamine from the absence of a clinical-trial basis for oral Ketamine.
Consider adverse effects and uncertain durability before offering intravenous treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: ketamine
alternative_regimens.summary: Sub-anesthetic intravenous administration reduced CRPS symptoms in two randomized trials, but the guideline identifies inadequate long-term outcome data and reports that tolerance and unpleasant psychoactive effects may limit treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients after consideration of evidence limitations and tolerability.

not_recommended.name: High-dose ketamine coma
not_recommended.reason: The guideline says it cannot be recommended because it is likely associated with very serious adverse effects.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain benefit, its duration, dysphoria, hallucinations, and other adverse effects.
response_assessment.interpretation: A temporary response should not be taken as evidence of durable efficacy.

supportive_care: Continue rehabilitation-oriented treatment.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The two positive trials examined 10 consecutive outpatient infusions and a 4.5 day inpatient course, respectively. The guideline states that oral Ketamine lacks a supporting clinical-trial evidence base.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with localized or focal symptoms for whom topical treatment is considered.
decision_rules: Consider topical treatment for suitable local symptoms while distinguishing it from transdermal medication that produces systemic exposure.
Assess local tolerability, particularly with capsaicin.

alternative_regimens.name: 5% lidocaine patch
alternative_regimens.summary: May help some local or focal CRPS symptoms, including allodynia; its cited approval concerns PHN rather than CRPS.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Localized symptoms amenable to a patch.

alternative_regimens.name: Eutectic Mixture of Local Anesthetics (EMLA)
alternative_regimens.summary: Some clinicians endorse its use in CRPS; application under an occlusive covering is needed for penetration.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A selected topical anesthetic option.

alternative_regimens.name: DMSO
alternative_regimens.summary: A systematic review reported reduced CRPS symptoms compared with placebo using 50% cream for 2 months, without improvement in pain intensity.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider the distinction between overall symptoms and the absence of demonstrated pain-intensity improvement.

response_assessment.method: Assess the targeted local symptom, skin reactions, and tolerability.
response_assessment.interpretation: Local irritation or lack of useful symptom improvement limits suitability.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Topical capsaicin has preliminary evidence of partial efficacy in CRPS when paired with regional anesthesia, but the guideline reports that application can be intolerably painful and that exacerbated CRPS pain may make it unsuitable.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with dystonia, severe edema, or other symptoms requiring treatment alongside general rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Treat painful dystonia as a distinct problem when it interferes with movement or tissue perfusion.
Treat severe edema with standard measures when tolerated.

recommended_regimens.name: baclofen
recommended_regimens.summary: The guideline identifies oral baclofen as the current first-line option for dystonia, while noting sedation and limited tolerance of effective high oral doses.

recommended_regimens.name: Limb elevation, regular aerobic exercise, and compressive garments
recommended_regimens.summary: Use standard measures for severe limb edema, applying compression if the patient tolerates it.

alternative_regimens.name: trihexylphenidate
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered for dystonia.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: An alternative to the guideline's first-line oral baclofen option.

alternative_regimens.name: Intrathecal baclofen
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered when baclofen helps dystonia but effective oral dosing is poorly tolerated; pharmacological and mechanical complications are common, and the original research group largely ceased using the approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients with a dystonic component and difficulty tolerating oral baclofen.

not_recommended.name: Long-term benzodiazepines or cyclobenzaprine for CRPS muscle symptoms
not_recommended.reason: The guideline describes these muscle relaxants as empirically ineffective and poorly tolerated over the long term.

response_assessment.method: Assess dystonic posture, pain, movement, edema, and treatment tolerance.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent severe dystonia or intolerable oral treatment may prompt consideration of another approach.

supportive_care: Integrate symptom-directed treatment with functional rehabilitation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Prolonged dystonic postures can progress to fixed contractures; severe edema can compromise tissue nutrition and integrity.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe pain or a suspected sympathetically maintained component that obstructs active rehabilitation.
decision_rules: Consider a sympathetic block empirically in selected patients when temporary pain relief could enable movement and rehabilitation.
Assess pain and functional response rather than assuming that vasomotor evidence of sympatholysis establishes analgesic success.
Do not assume that all patients with CRPS have sympathetically maintained pain.

alternative_regimens.name: Sympathetic nerve blockade
alternative_regimens.summary: Local-anesthetic blockade may provide a rehabilitation window for selected responders. One small blinded crossover study found longer mean analgesia with local anesthetic than saline, but systematic-review evidence did not establish effectiveness across broadly defined CRPS groups.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients whose block-related analgesia and functional improvement facilitate active treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Stellate ganglion block
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used for upper-extremity CRPS as part of a short course combined with active reanimation when an individual response supports doing so.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected upper-extremity patients with useful response.

alternative_regimens.name: Lumbar sympathetic block
alternative_regimens.summary: May be used for lower-extremity CRPS with active physiotherapy in selected responders, although the guideline highlights limited good evidence for this approach.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected lower-extremity patients with useful response.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain relief, duration, function, and ability to participate in rehabilitation, alongside signs of sympatholysis.
response_assessment.interpretation: Vasomotor change alone does not reliably establish complete blockade or predict analgesia.

supportive_care: Pair a useful analgesic interval with active rehabilitation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In Price et al.'s seven-patient comparison, mean relief lasted 3 d, 18h with local anesthetic versus 19h with saline. The guideline describes the overall therapeutic role of sympathetic blocks as largely empirical.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients needing sustained regional analgesia to permit active treatment, including selected patients for whom intermittent blocks are inadequate.
decision_rules: Titrate regional analgesia to allow participation in rehabilitation without unnecessary motor impairment.
Consider infection and other catheter-related risks when selecting or continuing an infusion.

alternative_regimens.name: Continuous brachial plexus infusion
alternative_regimens.summary: An upper-limb regional technique that can deliver local anesthetic and selected adjuvants while supporting active therapy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected upper-extremity patients requiring continuous regional analgesia.

alternative_regimens.name: Epidural infusion
alternative_regimens.summary: Adjust anesthetic concentration and infusion rate to balance analgesia with movement and physiotherapy; the guideline describes it as a possible next option after inadequate intermittent blocks.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients needing titratable continuous analgesia.

alternative_regimens.name: Epidural clonidine
alternative_regimens.summary: A cited randomized trial and subsequent open-label treatment reported analgesia, but adverse effects and catheter infections occurred.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Selected patients for whom an epidural approach is justified after weighing risks.

response_assessment.method: Monitor pain, active participation, sensory and motor effects, catheter site, and signs of infection.
response_assessment.interpretation: Adjust analgesia to preserve rehabilitation and evaluate suspected infection promptly.

supportive_care: For longer-term epidural catheters, use surgical sterility measures, tunnel the catheter away from the spinal entry site, and change dressings weekly.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Reported infection rates for epidural catheters used in CRPS reach as high as 31%. The guideline identifies back pain, sensorimotor loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction as features of epidural abscess, with fever, neck pain, or photophobia possible earlier symptoms. Its discussion of epidural clonidine contains differing dose and treatment-duration figures, so those figures are not combined into a regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with continuing substantial functional limitation or deterioration despite conservative and more intensive noninvasive treatment.
decision_rules: Consider neurostimulation after insufficient progress with functional restoration; explain risks, expected benefits, and alternatives through shared decision-making.
Use a successful temporary trial to determine whether permanent implantation is appropriate.
Interpret pain relief separately from functional improvement.

alternative_regimens.name: Spinal cord stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: May provide pain relief in selected patients after inadequate conservative treatment; the guideline notes that corroborating high-quality evidence is still needed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Persistent limitations after noninvasive treatment, particularly when blocks have not helped or are inappropriate.

alternative_regimens.name: Dorsal root ganglion stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: An advanced stimulation option for selected refractory CRPS, with comparative randomized evidence in chronic intractable lower-limb pain.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider for suitable focal lower-limb CRPS after inadequate conservative care and a successful trial.

response_assessment.method: In the ACCURATE study, trial success required at least a 50% reduction in VAS lower-limb pain and no new neurological complaints.
response_assessment.interpretation: Participants meeting the study's trial criteria proceeded to permanent implantation.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain, function, quality of life, medication use, and device-related problems.
response_assessment.interpretation: Pain improvement does not necessarily entail clinically significant functional improvement.

supportive_care: Continue functional rehabilitation and coordinated care.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Kemler et al.'s randomized study found pain reduction at 6-month follow-up with spinal cord stimulation plus physical therapy but no clinically significant functional gain. In the ACCURATE lower-limb trial, the primary endpoint at 12 months reported treatment success of 81.2% with dorsal root ganglion stimulation versus 56.7% with conventional spinal cord stimulation. The appendix separately reports a 3months comparison of 81.2% versus 55.7%; these are distinct reported timepoint figures.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients considered for neurodestructive or highly invasive procedures after other approaches.
decision_rules: Try simpler, less invasive, less hazardous, and less costly interventions before experimental or highly invasive procedures.
If response remains inadequate, consider any further escalation alongside noninterventional treatment and repeated evaluation of risk, benefit, and expense.

alternative_regimens.name: Motor cortex stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: The guideline describes this as the most invasive intervention discussed and requires a trial before implantation; its role is experimental.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Only in the context of consideration of later, highly invasive treatment.

not_recommended.name: Neurodestructive sympathetic procedures as routine chronic-pain treatment
not_recommended.reason: The guideline says they are rarely recommended because they can aggravate pain or cause deafferentation syndromes and post-sympathectomy neuralgia.

not_recommended.name: Routine ablative sympathectomy
not_recommended.reason: High-quality evidence of benefit is lacking, and adverse effects are substantial relative to efficacy.

supportive_care: Maintain noninterventional treatment during any stepwise escalation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A cited review found initial surgical sympathectomy failure of up to 35%; the guideline also reports post-sympathectomy neuralgia of up to 44% in an open-sympathectomy series for causalgia. The role of radiofrequency ablation remains uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with CRPS.
decision_rules: Use active rehabilitation with psychological support when indicated, adapting treatment to the child and family.
Interpret reported outcomes in light of the limited study designs and multicomponent interventions.

recommended_regimens.name: Physical therapy combined with cognitive-behavioral therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: A pediatric randomized study evaluated physical therapy at different weekly frequencies, with cognitive-behavioral treatment provided to both groups.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the trial of 28 children, both the once-per-week and three-times-per-week groups improved significantly on five measures of pain and function; benefit was sustained in the majority.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Physical therapy once per week or three times per week in the cited trial.

alternative_regimens.name: Intensive physical therapy with psychological counseling
alternative_regimens.summary: A prospective pediatric case series used aerobic exercise, hydrotherapy, and desensitization, with psychological counseling for 77% of participants.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A multicomponent rehabilitation approach reported in pediatric clinical evidence.

response_assessment.method: Assess pain, movement, daily function, psychological barriers, and recurrence.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use functional and symptom change together rather than pain scores alone.

supportive_care: Involve family in education and support for reactivation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In the cited series of 103 children, the authors reported initial benefit from intensive physical therapy with a low rate of long-term symptoms or dysfunction. The appendix reports 92% symptom resolution at treatment end and 88% symptom-free at 2year follow-up for this series; these outcomes are attributed to the cited study, not to an established guideline-wide expectation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients progressing toward community participation, leisure activities, or a possible return to work.
decision_rules: Integrate meaningful activity and vocational goals with the rehabilitation program.
Address return-to-work planning early even when vocational rehabilitation is a later stage of functional restoration.
Match work duties and any restrictions to observed capacity; avoid activities likely to aggravate the condition or increase long-term pain.

recommended_regimens.name: Vocational Rehabilitation
recommended_regimens.summary: Assess job demands and capacities, coordinate with occupational therapy, consider work simulation or hardening and a graded trial of work, and specify restrictions or modifications when needed.

alternative_regimens.name: Recreational therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Use enjoyable, adapted activities to encourage movement, support rehabilitation goals, and rebuild participation in community and leisure activities.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A possible component of multidisciplinary care, based on clinical experience rather than published outcome studies.

response_assessment.timepoint: Before work release and during a graded work trial
response_assessment.method: Assess actual job demands, functional capacity, work behavior, and tolerance of progressively greater work time and effort.
response_assessment.interpretation: Use findings to determine suitable duties, restrictions, modifications, or alternative placement.

supportive_care: Coordinate vocational decisions among the counselor, occupational therapist, physical therapist, and physician.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline states that the CRPS-specific value of recreational therapy and vocational rehabilitation rests on clinical experience rather than formal intervention studies.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients after limb fracture or surgery who are being considered for prevention of CRPS.
decision_rules: Do not treat preventive benefit from vitamin C as established: earlier favorable studies and a later large negative trial conflict.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Earlier analyses suggested 500 mg vitamin C daily for at least 45days after injury or surgery. A later large randomized trial using that protocol found an increased CRPS incidence at 6 weeks after fracture compared with placebo and no effect at later timepoints. The guideline therefore describes preventive utility as unproven.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Research on Complex Regional Pain Syndrome (CRPS) has advanced modestly, but most studies remain small and of low to medium quality; work on dorsal root ganglion stimulation is a notable exception. Because CRPS is rare, multifactorial and difficult to study in adequately powered samples, the authors used a semi-systematic review, supplemented where necessary by narrative assessment, case series, case reports and clinical experience. Broad diagnostic groupings based on the “Budapest” criteria may have obscured treatment-responsive subsets in larger trials. The authors favor tailoring treatment to each patient while stronger evidence is developed.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: This fifth edition addresses diagnosis and treatment of CRPS, also called Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy (RSD) or causalgia. Specialists in the disciplines involved in CRPS care reviewed relevant literature systematically but also considered preliminary research, clinical experience and, when necessary, evidence from related conditions. High-quality CRPS treatment research remains limited. The guidelines support, rather than replace, clinical judgment informed by training and individual circumstances. The authors acknowledge possible preferences for their own therapeutic approaches. Evidence levels are supplied where appropriate, and clinical choices require individual appraisal of risks, costs and benefits.

document_sections.heading: Diagnosis
document_sections.content: RSD and Causalgia are historical names sometimes applied inappropriately; neither has validated diagnostic criteria. The name CRPS arose from an international meeting in 1994, followed by consensus criteria adopted by the IASP. Subsequent validation studies led to empirically developed “Budapest Criteria,” formally adopted by the IASP taxonomy committee in 2012. Variation between patients and within the same patient over time complicates diagnostic classification.

document_sections.heading: Table 1. Levels of evidence (modified by consensus: used in prior versions and in this review [3])
document_sections.content: The table defines the review’s evidence hierarchy: Level 1 covers meta-analyses or systematic reviews; Level 2 covers adequately powered randomized controlled trials or statistically systematic studies validating criteria; Level 3 covers retrospective investigations, open-label trials and small pilot studies; and Level 4 covers anecdotes, case reports, clinical experience and empirical observations.

document_sections.heading: Table 2. Revised CRPS criteria adopted by the IASP in 2012 [3, 8]
document_sections.content: The table sets out the syndrome’s features and clinical diagnostic requirements. CRPS involves continuing regional spontaneous and/or evoked pain apparently disproportionate in duration or intensity to the expected course of an injury or lesion; its distribution is not confined to a nerve or dermatome, distal sensory, motor, sudomotor, vasomotor and/or trophic abnormalities commonly predominate, and its course varies. Diagnosis requires continuing disproportionate pain; at least one reported symptom in three of four categories; at least one observed sign in two or more categories at evaluation; and no better explanation for the findings. The categories are sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema and motor/trophic. Symptoms encompass hyperalgesia or allodynia; temperature or color asymmetry or color changes; edema or altered or asymmetric sweating; and reduced movement, weakness, tremor, dystonia, or changes involving hair, nails or skin. Corresponding signs must be observed, with sensory examination including pinprick hyperalgesia or allodynia to light touch, deep pressure or joint movement. A sign counts only when present at diagnosis.

document_sections.heading: Validation Studies
document_sections.content: Multisite validation compared patients meeting the 1994 IASP criteria with patients who had non-CRPS neuropathic pain (level 2 evidence). Standardized assessment and principal component analysis found four distinct clinical clusters rather than the two implicitly assumed by the 1994 criteria. Combining vasomotor with sudomotor/edema findings probably reduced specificity; motor and trophic findings were missing from those criteria; and signs and symptoms supplied potentially complementary diagnostic information. In a larger discrimination study, the 1994 criteria had sensitivity 0.98 and specificity 0.36, with a positive diagnosis potentially correct in as few as 40% of cases. A revised rule requiring positive findings in at least two of four sign categories and at least three of four symptom categories yielded sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.69. An independent study (level 2) found sensitivity 0.99 and specificity 0.68 for the “Budapest criteria.” Following review in Budapest in 2003, the IASP adopted the revised criteria in 2012. Clarifications were being incorporated into ICD-11. The criteria were designed as broad, inclusive and accessible screening-type criteria, not as a way to identify a single disease mechanism.

document_sections.heading: Table 3. Factors (and factor loadings) resulting from principal components analysis of diagnostic and associated signs and symptoms of CRPS, reused by permission from [9]
document_sections.content: The table displays four factors derived from CRPS signs and symptoms and their factor loadings. A loading represents the association between an individual finding and its factor. These factors underpin the distinction between sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor/edema and motor/trophic diagnostic features.

document_sections.heading: CRPS Stages? CRPS Subtypes?
document_sections.content: The historical proposal of three progressive CRPS stages rests on clinical tradition rather than specific scientific confirmation (level 4). Cluster analyses did not support sequential stages (level 2): symptom duration was similar across three identified groups. One study described groups dominated by vasomotor findings, dominated by neuropathic pain and sensory abnormalities, or displaying a broad, more severe constellation resembling classic RSD; both studies identified statistical support for the severe group. An international prospective multisite analysis identified a warm, red, dry, edematous cluster and a cold, blue, sweaty, less edematous cluster (level 2). Median duration was 4.7 months in warm CRPS and 20months in cold CRPS, despite comparable pain intensity. Warm findings predominated early, but a small group with brief-duration cold findings was provisionally termed “primary cold CRPS.” Inflammatory-feature counts were significantly higher initially in the warm group and diminished significantly over a 3-month follow-up only in that group. A possible transition from an acute inflammatory warm presentation to a more stable cold presentation remains an interpretation, not an established sequence. Warm-versus-cold classification remains informal pending further research; clinicians should nevertheless record the predominant temperature pattern because of possible prognostic and treatment implications. No evidence indicates that subtyping removes the need for interdisciplinary care. The proposed formal category “CRPS with Remission of Some Features,” intended for ICD-11, applies only when full criteria were documented previously but are no longer met. Such patients may still have pain and other manifestations and may relapse; temporarily falling below diagnostic thresholds must not be equated with cure. The formal CRPS-Type I versus CRPS-Type II distinction, respectively without or with “major nerve damage,” was retained largely for historical reasons. Their principal diagnostic criteria overlap, the threshold for major nerve damage and the necessary tests are uncertain, and the distinction may have little clinical or therapeutic significance.

document_sections.heading: Beyond Dichotomous Diagnosis: Assessment of CRPS Symptom Severity
document_sections.content: A yes-or-no diagnosis does not measure severity or treatment-related change. The CRPS Severity Score (CSS), introduced in 2010 (level 2), uses findings from the 2012 IASP criteria and needs no specialized training or equipment. Its 16 elements comprise 8 signs and 8 symptoms recorded as present or absent from history and examination, producing a possible score of 0–16. Higher CSS scores were significantly associated with diagnosis, greater pain, distress and functional impairment, and distinguished CRPS from non-CRPS neuropathic pain. In cross-validation (level 2), scores were comparatively stable in established chronic disease but changed significantly more during initial treatment of acute disease. Score changes were significantly associated with simultaneous changes in pain, fatigue and functioning. A change of 5 or more CSS scale points appears clinically significant.

document_sections.heading: The Development of an International Core Data Set and Clinical Research Registry for CRPS
document_sections.content: The IRC was established in 2015 to facilitate CRPS research. Low incidence, heterogeneous patients, small studies and inconsistent outcome measures impede synthesis and sufficiently powered collaborative investigations. An international registry with standardized outcomes could help investigate risk factors, subtypes, mechanisms and treatment effectiveness. A consortium established in 2013 brought together patients, researchers, clinicians and industry participants from 20 countries across Europe, the Americas, Asia and Africa. Its initiative, COMPACT, seeks an agreed core data set and international clinical research registry; the Royal United Hospitals Bath NHS Foundation Trust leads this work. Registry development remains ongoing.

document_sections.heading: A CRPS Core Data Set.
document_sections.content: A core outcome set specifies minimum standardized measures for research in a condition. COMPACT includes demographic information, patient-reported questionnaires, clinician-reported questionnaires and clinical measures still being developed. Its initial questionnaire selection drew on a PubMed systematic review (level 1 evidence), a professional survey (level 4 evidence) and international workshop consensus. Patient-reported domains address pain, disease severity, participation and function, emotional and psychological functioning, sleep, self-efficacy, catastrophizing and perceived change; the clinician-reported measure includes the CSS. A subsequent two-stage eDelphi process considered which clinical measures should be mandatory or optional. Its findings were discussed at a workshop in Valencia in September 2019 and were being prepared for publication.

document_sections.heading: Table 4. COMPACT data set
document_sections.content: The table identifies the patient-reported and clinician-reported instruments, demographic items, the constructs they assess and clinical measures still in development. PROMIS-29 covers 7 domains; the pain intensity numeric rating scale records the least and worst pain over the preceding 24hours; and CRPS symptom questions derive from the Budapest diagnostic criteria.

document_sections.heading: Development of a CRPS Clinical Research Registry.
document_sections.content: A multicenter feasibility study conducted during 2019–2021 assessed international collection of COMPACT questionnaires and use of ALEA for electronic registry data. Participants came from Brazil, Israel, Japan, Switzerland, the USA and the UK; translations followed a best-practice protocol where needed. The study’s conduct and findings were being prepared for publication. Recruitment to the international registry was anticipated in 2022. An initial international survey found broad variation in questionnaire selection; repeating it after registry establishment was planned to assess uptake of the core data set. The IRC website was designated to provide future information on recruitment and research access.

document_sections.heading: Interdisciplinary Management
document_sections.content: The rehabilitation review searched PubMed and MEDLINE without a date restriction, prioritizing relevant, higher-quality studies while also incorporating practical and anecdotal information. Consensus work in Malibu in 1997 placed functional restoration at the center of treatment, with medicines, blocks and psychotherapy added when progress was inadequate; its updated algorithm includes newer approaches. Interdisciplinary or multidisciplinary pain care emphasizing function is considered particularly effective for chronic pain (level 1), although the Malibu algorithm itself has not undergone a feasible controlled trial. Proposed progression starts with motor imagery and visual-tactile discrimination, advances to gentle active movement and partial loading (level 4), then to more demanding scrub-and-carry loading (level 3). Gradual sensory desensitization accompanies increasing function; its proposed effect on central processing is supported at level 3. Edema control and general aerobic activity are important (level 4). If progress stalls, additional measures may create enough comfort or confidence to continue: blocks may permit therapy despite severe allodynia, and cognitive behavioral methods may address kinesiophobia. Significant depression, anxiety or pain preventing therapy can justify medication, blocks or psychotherapy from the outset rather than waiting for failure.

document_sections.heading: The Rationale for Functional Restoration
document_sections.content: CRPS has varying peripheral, central and psychosocial features that can change with time; its epidemiology, natural history and treatment evidence remain incompletely understood. The authors favor an orderly interdisciplinary approach involving coordinated, specially trained professionals who regularly review and adapt care; multidisciplinary care coordinated by one clinician is more accessible but less integrated. Judging whether pain is disproportionate is necessary yet subjective for both clinician and patient, and pain reports may reflect biological, psychological and social circumstances. Psychological comorbidities deserve assessment and treatment, but CRPS is not a psychological disorder, and neither psychological scores nor pain ratings alone are suitable primary measures of rehabilitation success. The proposed central benchmark is stepwise, measurable functional restoration. International consensus work supports that emphasis, while a Dutch guideline reports benefit from physical therapy for function and coping and recommends it as standard CRPS care. IMMPACT identifies physical functioning as a core pain-treatment outcome. Functional restoration progressively emphasizes movement, desensitization, normalized use and participation in work or study. Which components, timing, duration and delivery methods are effective has not yet been adequately established.

document_sections.heading: Evidence
document_sections.content: Evidence for reanimation and functional restoration is modest. A 1997 meta-analysis (level 1) identified small CRPS trials with fewer placebo controls, less blinding and less statistical testing than neuropathic-pain trials. An uncontrolled 1988 RSD study (level 3) showed that functional and biometric measures could be tracked over time, changed during interdisciplinary rehabilitation and accompanied reductions in pain. Uncontrolled work suggested benefit from stress loading and isometric methods (level 4). A controlled study of 135 patients with upper-extremity CRPS found PT and OT useful for pain, mobility and impairment (level 2); a meta-analysis (level 1) favored pain-focused PT plus medical care over control treatment. In another prospective assessment of 145 patients, those receiving PT had less pain (level 3). Exercise reduced or eliminated pain in 92% of a study’s 28 children (level 3). Immobilization, muscle spasm, guarding and disuse may contribute to pain and disability and warrant assessment and active rehabilitation. A meta-analysis reported good to very good evidence for clinically meaningful, lasting pain reduction with graded motor imagery plus medical management (level 2). Mirror treatment had promising pilot results (level 3), and a trial in 48 stroke patients with CRPS found less pain and better upper-limb motor function than control treatment (level 2). Small studies of sensorimotor retuning and vibratory feedback reported less pain and improved proprioception (level 3); one desensitization study also observed more normal sensory-cortex organization. Whether normalized movement reverses central changes remains partly hypothetical. Casting healthy participants for 28days produced CRPS-like findings, and animal immobilization work found autonomic disturbance and allodynia. There is currently no level 1 or 2 evidence specifically establishing interdisciplinary CRPS treatment. An observational interdisciplinary-program cohort of 49 patients improved function in the short term; 14 out of 16 workers’ compensation patients returned to work (level 3). Meta-analyses in broader chronic-pain populations support interdisciplinary management (level 1), but comparable effectiveness specifically in CRPS remains unproven. Suggested brain-function barriers to functional treatment in CRPS remain speculative.

document_sections.heading: Principles of Functional Restoration
document_sections.content: Restoration combines patient motivation, desensitization, progressive reactivation, symptom-directed medicines or procedures, and cognitive behavioral methods. The Malibu group also proposed formal treatment guidance (level 3). Its original framework did not establish optimal intervention sequence or duration. Its suggestion that patients advance through each level in 2 weeks or less proved overly rigid, and reserving medication, blocks and psychological care until rehabilitation stalls overlooks patients who need these measures at the beginning. Multiple concurrent interventions are often needed to initiate restoration.

document_sections.heading: Interdisciplinary versus Multidisciplinary
document_sections.content: The authors regard closely coordinated interdisciplinary team care as central to CRPS management, although access is limited. They report that their urban 4 week program costs 1/3 to 1/2 as much as one spinal cord stimulator implantation, excluding device maintenance or replacement. When interdisciplinary care is unavailable, coordinated multidisciplinary referrals led by an informed clinician are preferable to a single-discipline approach, despite the workload and weaker team integration. In August 2001, the Minneapolis Group revised the Malibu framework to favor concurrent rehabilitation, pain-management and psychological pathways when appropriate, permit more flexible analgesia and timing, and preserve functional outcomes as the priority. Both groups treated pain as important for setting intervention type and pace while considering function a more objective principal outcome.

document_sections.heading: Occupational Therapy
document_sections.content: OT evaluates affected-limb use, active movement, edema, dexterity, vasomotor and sensory findings, pain and activities of daily living. Treatment may begin with graded motor imagery (GMI) or mirror visual feedback (MVF). A study (level 3) found MVF beneficial in early and intermediate CRPS but no significant effect in chronic CRPS. GMI progresses through laterality recognition, imagined movement and mirror viewing. The mechanisms of GMI and MVF remain uncertain, and treatment should follow symptoms and individual response. The MVF home approach emphasizes sessions lasting no more than 5 minutes, repeated 5–6 times throughout the day. The described GMI program lasts 6-week, with 2weeks in each phase. Inability to experience ownership of the mirrored limb, greater pain or worsening movement disorders are identified contraindications. A small randomized GMI trial (n= 13; intervention n =7; level 2) found significantly greater pain improvement than standard treatment, but larger subsequent studies did not confirm pain benefit and one suggested increased pain and edema. A controlled pilot of virtual body swapping improved body-perception disturbance briefly without significantly changing pain (level 3). Definitive clinical value remains uncertain. Subsequent OT goals are edema reduction, normalized sensation and positioning, less guarding, and greater independence in work, leisure and daily activities. Functional splinting may help severe cases, but sustained splinting can aggravate symptoms. Edema garments, manual mobilization and superficial desensitization are described at level 4. Stress loading combines scrubbing with progressively heavier carrying. Symptoms can initially rise before pain and swelling usually begin to fall after several days. Loading amount and duration increase gradually; the DystrophileV has no demonstrated advantage over a simple brush. The clinical usefulness of stress loading remains supported mainly at level 4, and comparative efficacy requires study. With improved edema and loading tolerance, treatment advances to active movement, coordination and strengthening; PNF patterns may aid strength, balance and everyday activities. Programs should be adjusted to response. OT and vocational counseling should jointly assess work demands and possible accommodations. Job-site analysis, conditioning, capacity assessment, transferable skills review and trial work periods should be considered. Work releases should specify relevant physical limitations, especially for sedentary or light duties; these vocational recommendations are level 4.

document_sections.heading: Physical Therapy
document_sections.content: PT complements other rehabilitation disciplines and gradually develops movement, flexibility, strength, gait and functional activity. Exercise should remain within tolerance, never be performed while the limb is insensate after a block or in CRPS Type II with marked hypoesthesia, and avoid excessive intensity that may provoke pain, edema, distress, fatigue and worsening inflammatory or sympathetic findings. Excessive inactivity, prolonged ice and some assistive or movement devices may also aggravate CRPS. Trials in upper-limb CRPS found better pain and active mobility with PT, and less marked benefit with OT, than counseling alone (level 2). Treatment should promote patient control, coping, normal posture and movement, and prevention of compensatory changes. Early graded exercise may preserve function and shorten disease duration. In children, a trial comparing PT plus cognitivebehavioral therapy once per week with three times per week found significant improvement in both groups across five pain and function measures, sustained for the majority (level 2). A series of 103 children reported benefit from intensive PT supplemented by psychological counseling in 77%, with low long-term symptom or dysfunction rates (level 3). Activity should balance excessive exercise against prolonged rest, incorporating pacing and relaxation. Preliminary graded exposure work suggests reduced disability through less fear of movement (level 3). A time-contingent Pain Exposure Therapy case series of 20 patients reported reduced pain and functional limitations (level 3), but the approach is controversial. Gentle mat and Feldenkrais exercises, proprioceptive training, graded sensorimotor retuning and vibratory stimulation have varying preliminary support. In a six-patient cohort, sensorimotor retuning showed preliminary benefit (level 3); a pilot comparing 7 recipients of 80– 100 Hz vibration plus PT with n =4 receiving PT alone found greater improvements in pain and movement in the vibration group (level 3). Myofascial pain should be treated actively (level 4), although the assertion that treating it first might resolve CRPS is unproven. Aquatic therapy may facilitate edema reduction and early loading; excessively hot or cold water can worsen symptoms. Gentle massage may sometimes relieve myofascial pain or edema, but lacks controlled evidence (level 4); electrostimulation has only clinical-experience support, and ultrasound has appeared less effective. Mild contrast baths might help early disease, but cold immersion can worsen advanced CRPS: contrast baths are not recommended in advanced cases and have little empirical support at any duration. Most modality-specific PT evidence remains level 3–4, and better studies are needed.

document_sections.heading: Recreational Therapy
document_sections.content: This discussion rests on clinical experience rather than published outcome studies. Enjoyable activities, adaptations and participation in preferred pastimes may help patients move an affected limb, address kinesiophobia, practice desensitization or loading, and reconnect socially. Recreational therapists can coordinate tasks with PT and OT goals, including dexterity, range of motion, gait and community activity. Proposed psychological and quality-of-life benefits have not been established by systematic CRPS research. Limited reimbursement may require PT or OT practitioners to cover this role.

document_sections.heading: Vocational Rehabilitation
document_sections.content: The proposed role of vocational rehabilitation (VR) is based on clinical experience, without formal studies establishing its specific CRPS benefit. VR assesses whether a patient can resume the original job, a modified role, another position with the same employer or new employment. Assessment may involve job descriptions, employer consultation, site visits, job-specific conditioning, work-capacity and functional evaluations, and transferable-skills assessment. VR should coordinate closely with OT and the wider team. Social, educational and employment circumstances may influence work disability alongside health. Although VR is often late in rehabilitation, addressing employment early establishes a longer-term goal. A graded trial of work can reveal capacity and reduce anxiety; returning to work may itself be therapeutic if duties do not aggravate CRPS or increase long-term pain. Releases for restricted, sedentary or light work should give specific limitations and consider physical demands, repetitive tasks, temperature and vibration. The benefit of VR in CRPS has not been systematically tested.

document_sections.heading: Other Therapeutic Interventions of Note
document_sections.content: A medium-sized randomized trial found hyperbaric oxygen reduced pain and edema significantly more than normal air (level 2), but replication and cost-benefit assessment are needed. Of two acupuncture RCTs, a small study (n=14) found no significant outcome difference; a larger study (n= 96) reported better pain severity and affected-limb motor function 40days after treatment for post-stroke CRPS type I (level 2). Its clinical utility requires more research. Case studies suggest possible improvement in pain, movement and function after chiropractic manipulation (level 4). Overall, the authors favor systematic, empathetic interdisciplinary care, or multidisciplinary care when necessary. Functional restoration as the central intervention and outcome remains a proposition requiring testing.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: Few medications commonly used in CRPS have been adequately tested in high-quality blinded RCTs. Past diagnostic inconsistency, low prevalence and limited incentives to study older drugs have constrained research. The clinician may draw cautiously on evidence from related neuropathic conditions and conduct patient-specific empirical trials without prolonging ineffective treatments. CRPS also involves microcirculatory, bone and inflammatory processes and does not meet current neuropathic-pain criteria merely because its pain can have neuropathic qualities. Mechanisms vary across patients and time, making a single universally effective medicine unlikely. Drugs studied specifically for CRPS include calcitonin, bisphosphonates and immune-modulating treatments; other agents have mainly been studied in neuropathic pain. Medication is most useful alongside functional restoration and management of comorbidity.

document_sections.heading: General Considerations
document_sections.content: Patients should understand that no treatment is proven to cure CRPS or help everyone, although medicines can help some individuals. Early CRPS of up to 6-18 months duration may respond differently from persistent disease and often improves naturally; temporary benefit may support recovery. Approximately 15% of early cases do not recover, and an early cold limb may indicate poorer prognosis. Analgesic tolerance may develop while adverse effects persist. Monotherapy is preferred where possible, but carefully chosen combinations from different classes may be necessary; costs and individual needs matter. Drugs addressing several symptoms can be useful. Whether selected as-needed dosing better limits tolerance than scheduled dosing remains uncertain. Patient and clinician should agree on achievable goals before starting, such as a two-point reduction on a 0–10 pain scale or improved specified activities. Treatment should be reconsidered if goals are unmet or benefit wanes.

document_sections.heading: Anti-Inflammatory Drugs
document_sections.content: NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors, corticosteroids and free-radical scavengers have potentially relevant anti-inflammatory actions, but CRPS inflammation may be neurogenic and no drug has proved effective against that particular process. Inflammatory findings may improve spontaneously without parallel pain improvement. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and prostaglandin synthesis; prophylactic or rescue use has not been directly evaluated in CRPS trials. The authors report benefit in some patients from clinical experience (level 4 evidence), including possible benefit for secondary proximal myofascial pain. Research support is limited, and one CRPS study found no analgesic value. Ketoprofen may have additional anti-bradykinin and anti-prostacyclin activity. Selective COX-2 inhibitors such as celecoxib have not been tested in CRPS; reports of benefit are anecdotal (level 4 evidence), and cardiac concerns constrain use. Acetaminophen is not currently recommended for chronic disease treatment because regular or high-dose use can cause liver toxicity.

document_sections.heading: Immune Modulation
document_sections.content: Some level 2 evidence suggests that steroids begun very soon after trauma at approximately 30mg/day for 2–12 weeks, followed by tapering, may help, although a systematic review rated one trial low quality. A short course may be appropriate for early inflammatory CRPS; benefit from longer courses is unproven, and chronic steroid use has serious contraindications. In persistent CRPS, intermediate-dose oral steroids totaling 1 g over 2weeks rarely help and often cause adverse effects. Intravenous pulsed dosing of 3x1g iv has not been assessed; one intrathecal injection proved ineffective. An initial persistent-CRPS RCT (level 2) suggested benefit with IVIG at 0.5 g/kg, but a larger subsequent trial was negative. High-dose IVIG has anecdotal support only. A preliminary infliximab RCT stopped early and found no benefit (level 3); a large persistent-CRPS lenalidomide RCT likewise found no benefit (level 2). A small open-label randomized study suggested benefit with mycophenolate 1.5g BID (level 3), requiring confirmation. Case series reported benefit with plasma exchange (level 4), but the authors’ experience indicates repeated courses, for example eight exchanges over 4weeks, and frequent pain at venous access. A low-dose naltrexone trial was recruiting. In a preliminary Cetuximab study (level 3), 4/7 treated patients appeared to improve versus 2/7 after placebo. Combining immune therapies and targeting autoantibodies or their downstream effects remain possibilities without definitive CRPS trials; other agents are prospective research candidates (level 4).

document_sections.heading: Bisphosphonates
document_sections.content: Bisphosphonates affect immune activity and bone metabolism. One RCT involving very early CRPS, with average duration 5 weeks after trauma, found some efficacy (level 2), but it has not been replicated. Small persistent-CRPS trials reported benefit, whereas two recent larger industry-sponsored studies were either unpublished or negative (level 2). Possible efficacy in selected subtypes needs confirmation in RCTs, particularly because rare serious adverse effects occur (level 4). The proposed greater benefit in patients with osteopenia identifiable through bone density or triple phase bone scanning remains unproven (level 4).

document_sections.heading: Cation-Channel Blockers
document_sections.content: Neuronal sodium- or calcium-entry blockers have substantial evidence in other neuropathic pain conditions (level 1 evidence), but CRPS-specific findings are limited. Gabapentin acts at the alpha(2)-delta auxiliary subunit of voltage-dependent calcium channels and has demonstrated efficacy in postherpetic neuralgia and diabetic neuropathy (level 2 evidence). CRPS case reports and series suggest possible benefit (level 4 evidence), whereas its sole CRPS RCT was negative at a sub-maximal 1800mg/day (level 2). Pregabalin has essentially the same described mode of action and may permit twice-daily administration for some patients, but costs differ and no CRPS trial data exist. A preliminary study suggested some analgesic effect of carbamazepine 600 mg/day over 8 days in selected CRPS patients. Oxcarbazepine may cause fewer serious adverse effects than carbamazepine but can cause headache, dizziness and nausea; it has not been studied specifically in CRPS. Phenytoin has many adverse effects and no reported CRPS outcomes. Lamotrigine has not been trialed for CRPS. Evidence for levetiracetam and topiramate in CRPS is anecdotal (level 4), without compelling clinical trials.

document_sections.heading: Augmentation of Monoamines
document_sections.content: Tricyclic and heterocyclic drugs inhibit monoamine reuptake and can address neuralgic pain, depression, anxiety or insomnia. Evidence from neuropathic pain includes meta-analyses (level 1), but their trials lasted only weeks to a few months and longer-term tolerance may occur. One report estimated that among every 100 neuropathic-pain patients receiving antidepressants, 30 achieve at least 50% pain relief, corresponding to an NNT of 3. Some clinicians consider as-needed use in persistent CRPS to delay tolerance, particularly for difficult nights. Drug choice may exploit differing sedative or activating effects: examples given are doxepin and desipramine. SSRIs have not demonstrated analgesic efficacy (level 4 evidence), although they are useful for anxiety and depression; reported neuropathic-pain NNT values are 7.7 for citalopram and 2.9 for paroxetine. The authors consider tricyclic/heterocyclic drugs particularly valuable individual agents for CRPS but advise low starting doses, gradual escalation and close monitoring; a low-dose trial alone should not establish ineffectiveness. They recommend an EKG before reaching the mid-dose range and at the ultimate dose because interval changes can occur (level 4). SNRIs including venlafaxine, milnacipran and duloxetine have not been trialed for CRPS. Venlafaxine has anecdotal value for neuropathic pain and possibly CRPS (level 4 evidence); comparative CRPS efficacy and safety data for SNRIs and TCAs are needed.

document_sections.heading: Opioids
document_sections.content:
Opioids may provide substantial short-term relief but present important longer-term problems. The sole CRPS RCT (level 2) found no difference in pain reduction between controlled-release morphine and placebo after 8 days’ use; because that trial would not meet current quality standards, short-term efficacy remains unresolved. Escalating doses in neuropathic pain may add adverse effects without additional relief. Patients prescribed 100 mg or more of daily morphine equivalent had a 9 times greater serious-overdose risk than those prescribed less than 20mg, after adjustment for comorbidities. A growing consensus regards lower-dose opioids as a possible 2nd or 3rd line trial, without unrestricted escalation. Methadone has proposed NMDA-related advantages and low cost; Tramadol and tapentadol have described monoamine-reuptake properties that may be useful. Long-term tolerance and toxicity in CRPS remain unresolved, while sustained high-dose use can worsen allodynia and/or hyperpathia. Although some individuals may use low doses successfully over time, analgesic tolerance often coexists with opioid-induced hyperalgesia that can resemble CRPS symptoms.
