Short-acting rescue doses remain controversial: occasional use for a flare differs from daily or near-daily use that effectively raises the standing dose and promotes tolerance.

Chronic opioid use carries established risks of illness and death. Because CRPS involves hyperalgesia and prolonged opioid treatment can itself cause hyperalgesia, the rationale for continued use is uncertain. Its risks and benefits must be reassessed continuously.

document_sections.heading: NMDA Receptor Antagonists
document_sections.content: NMDA receptor antagonists evaluated for neuropathic pain or CRPS include MK-801, ketamine, amantadine, memantine, and dextromethorphan; toxicity has generally been substantial at effective doses. Ketamine has been administered topically, orally, intra-nasally, intravenously, and intrathecally. Two CRPS RCTs found sub-anesthetic intravenous ketamine effective, using either 10 consecutive outpatient infusions or a 4.5 day inpatient course with gradually increased doses (level 2). Some centers provide low-dose intravenous Ketamine despite the absence of reliable long-term outcome data (level 4). In the authors’ experience, tolerance can shorten its benefit; dysphoria, hallucinations, and a drug “high” also deter patients (level 4). High-dose “ketamine coma” cannot be recommended because it is likely to cause very serious adverse effects. Clinical trial evidence does not support oral Ketamine. The positive intravenous trials suggest that central sensitization contributes to CRPS and may be temporarily reversible in many patients. Amantadine showed some benefit in cancer-related neuropathic pain (level 2) and chronic neuropathic pain (level 4). A small RCT suggested that oral Memantine combined with oral morphine helped a subgroup with persistent upper-limb CRPS, comprising 40% men and generally having low pain intensity; the authors’ attempt to reproduce this result in a more typical persistent-CRPS population found no indication of benefit.

document_sections.heading: Anti-Hypertensives and a-Adrenergic Antagonists
document_sections.content: Clonidine, an a2-adrenergic agonist, was used more often when sympathetically maintained pain was considered nearly universal in CRPS. Oral, transdermal, and epidural administration have been described (level 3 evidence). Reported adverse effects are sedation, dizziness, headache, and hypotension. A case series found improvement in local CRPS-related hyperalgesia and allodynia with transdermal clonidine (level 4 evidence), whereas a systematic review found no convincing support (level 1 evidence); its present use is rare. Nifedipine has a rationale for treating vasoconstriction (level 4 evidence), and two uncontrolled case series reported usefulness at up to 60 mg/day. Phenoxybenzamine and phentolamine are sometimes considered third-line treatments. Two case series offer preliminary support for phenoxybenzamine. Phentolamine is costly, scarce, administered by continuous intravenous infusion, and not widely used.

document_sections.heading: Calcitonin
document_sections.content: Calcitonin appears to benefit CRPS beyond its effects on bone. It is generally administered intra-nasally and has no significant adverse effects in people with normal calcium levels. Multiple RCTs have studied it; a meta-analysis of a limited number of controlled studies supports intranasal 100–300IU per day (level 1). Two other trials classified as high quality in a systematic review disagreed (level 2): one reported improved pain after 100 IU thrice daily for 3 weeks, whereas the other found no improvement after 200 IU twice daily for four weeks. Despite generally favorable level 1 evidence, calcitonin is seldom prescribed and is difficult to obtain.

document_sections.heading: Pharmacotherapy for Other Symptoms in Chronic CRPS
document_sections.content: CRPS-associated dystonia commonly needs separate treatment: it is painful, can impair tissue perfusion, and prolonged fixed postures can shorten tendons into contractures requiring painful orthopedic measures such as tendon release or serial casting. Treatments ordinarily used for dystonia are also prescribed in CRPS, although the proposed mechanisms differ from those of dystonias mediated by basalganglia dysfunction. Trihexylphenidate may be considered; baclofen is the current first-line choice (level 4). Oral baclofen should be tried first, but sedation limits tolerance of doses effective for dystonia. An intrathecal pump is sometimes considered when it works but cannot be tolerated orally; pharmacological and mechanical complications are common, and its original investigators have largely stopped using it. Prolonged use of benzodiazepines or cyclobenzaprine is empirically ineffective and poorly tolerated (level 4). In rare cases, severe limb edema painfully distorts tissues and impairs oxygenation and nutrition; skin ulceration, infection, and, in extremely rare and disputed circumstances, amputation may follow. Usual management consists of limb elevation, regular aerobic exercise, and compression garments when tolerated.

document_sections.heading: Emerging Drug Treatment Options
document_sections.content: Evidence for cannabinoids is emerging in peripheral and central neuropathic pain, especially pain associated with multiple sclerosis, but they have not been tested for CRPS. Increasing availability of medical marijuana and cannabinoids could make such a trial feasible. Botulinum toxin type A blocks acetylcholine release at cholinergic synapses and also inhibits release of other neurotransmitters and neuropeptides, including glutamate, substance P, and CGRP, from primary afferent terminals. Regional intradermal injections improved spontaneous pain, brush allodynia, and cold-pain thresholds in 25 patients with post-traumatic neuralgia. Combined with sympathetic bupivicaine blockade, it prolonged analgesia in a subset of CRPS patients (Level 3); confirmation is needed. Oral CGRP receptor antagonists have been effective and well tolerated for acute migraine. Because CGRP and other nociceptor secretions may initiate local CRPS features, the authors propose future CRPS assessment of these drugs.

document_sections.heading: Topical Treatments
document_sections.content: Unlike systemic transdermal delivery through fentanyl or clonidine patches, topical medicines act locally on skin structures. Their principal serious adverse effects are rash and allergy. Options considered for CRPS are the 5% lidocaine patch, capsaicin, and dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO), all with level 4 evidence for CRPS. Some clinicians favor Eutectic Mixture of Local Anesthetics (EMLA) (level 3 evidence); an occlusive covering is needed for maximal penetration. The 5% lidocaine patch is FDA-approved for PHN and might help focal CRPS manifestations such as allodynia (level 4). Capsaicin activates TRPV1 on nociceptive neurons and subsequently causes nociceptive endings to recede; burning during application limits use. An RCT found modest benefit in PHN (level 2), and a preliminary CRPS study combining high-dose topical capsaicin with regional anesthesia found partial efficacy (level 3). The authors find it excessively painful, messy, and unacceptable to most patients (level 4). The FDA approved an 8% capsaicin patch in 2009 for PHN once every 3months, applied for 1 hour after topical local anesthesia. Two further RCTs favored high- over low-dose capsaicin in peripheral neuropathic pain (level 2), but increased CRPS pain may make it unsuitable (level 4). DMSO scavenges free radicals. In a systematic review, 50% DMSO cream for 2 months significantly reduced CRPS symptoms against placebo but did not improve pain intensity (level 1).

document_sections.heading: Prevention
document_sections.content: Analysis and meta-analysis of the first four studies suggested that vitamin C lowered CRPS occurrence after limb fracture or surgery and recommended 500 mg daily for at least 45days. A subsequent large post-fracture RCT using that protocol instead found increased CRPS incidence at 6 weeks compared with placebo and no effect later. Preventive benefit therefore remains unproven. Few CRPS drug trials attain level 1 or level 2 evidence. Treatment must draw on neuropathic-pain RCTs, smaller CRPS studies, and clinical experience. The authors advocate individualized, systematic trials of one new medicine at a time, advancing to maximum dose and stopping when benefit is unclear or adverse effects intolerable. Supporting rehabilitation and functional restoration matters as much as pain relief.

document_sections.heading: Psychological Interventions
document_sections.content: Definitive medical treatment is lacking, and successful CRPS care is generally understood to address medical, psychological, and social dimensions together. This section examines proposed links between psychological processes and CRPS, CRPS-specific treatment studies, evidence from other chronic pain conditions, and clinical approaches; it does not characterize CRPS as a psychological disorder.

document_sections.heading: Hypothesized Links Between CRPS and Psychological Factors
document_sections.content: Psychological treatment is supported by its use in other chronic pain conditions and by hypothetical interactions with CRPS physiology. Peripheral nerve injury may reduce sympathetic outflow and increase local sensitivity to circulating catecholamines, contributing to vasoconstriction and the cool, blue limb sometimes seen in chronic CRPS. Adrenergically sensitive afferents might increase nociceptive input and central sensitization; pain could then promote further catecholamine release. Stress and negative emotion can increase catecholamines. In 16 CRPS patients, greater depressive symptoms accompanied higher plasma epinephrine. These proposed causal links remain theoretical. In healthy volunteers, greater pain catastrophizing accompanied increased pro-inflammatory cytokine activity during painful stimulation; in CRPS, psychological stress was associated with immune changes that might influence inflammation. A 2009 review found that most earlier studies did not support psychological factors as causes or maintainers of CRPS. Prospective fracture cohorts produced mixed findings: among 50 patients, CRPS incidence was 18% without significant differences in personality or depression scores; among 596 patients, 7% developed CRPS, with neither early depression nor stressful events predicting it. Before knee arthroplasty, higher anxiety predicted a significantly greater likelihood of CRPS diagnosis at one month, with a similar trend for depression. In that dataset, increases in depression by 4 weeks predicted more CSS symptoms at 6and 12-month follow-up; increased anxiety showed a similar association at 6months. These findings are ambiguous and do not imply that psychological risk factors alone are necessary or sufficient. Among 88 patients with acute distal radius fracture, 14 had high life stress but did not develop CRPS, whereas the one patient who developed it lacked evident psychological risk factors. Retrospective reports linked onset with loss or stress; one controlled retrospective study reported contemporaneous stressful events in 80% of CRPS patients versus 20% of controls. Pediatric retrospective findings and a study reporting pre-pain Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder in 86% of affected adults cannot establish causation. Prospective tests of the life-stress hypothesis are lacking. Another cross-sectional study found CRPS patients reported more stressful events than the general population but fewer than patients with conversion or affective disorders, without a distinctive childhood-trauma pattern. Structured interviews estimated Axis I disorder prevalence at 24% to 46%; the study with a non-CRPS pain control group did not find a significantly higher rate in CRPS. No compelling evidence establishes psychiatric disorders as causes or as uniquely prevalent in CRPS, although identified disorders should be treated. Some cross-sectional studies found more depression or anxiety than in other pain groups, while others found no difference; selection, pain duration, referral, and measurement may explain disagreement. Greater distress cannot presently be assigned a clear causal direction. Some studies found stronger relationships of pain with depression, anxiety, anger, and acute stress in CRPS than in other chronic pain. In a small prospective study, greater baseline anxiety predicted less pain relief and functional improvement 6-months or more after sympathetic blocks (level 3). Immobilization experiments in 30 healthy participants showed that 28days of casting produced cold hyperalgesia and temperature asymmetry lasting 3 days after removal, alongside longer-lasting reduction in mechanical pain threshold. Avoidance and learned disuse might maintain CRPS through altered sensory input and reduced limb movement, but proposed psychophysiological interactions remain largely speculative. Greater initial anxiety and pain-related fear predicted worse pain and disability over 12months in an acute-CRPS prospective study (level 3). An electronic diary study associated greater acceptance-based coping with better pain and mood on the same day. Psychological care may improve coping, function, self-management, and confidence in rehabilitation.

document_sections.heading: Efficacy of Psychological Interventions in CRPS Patients
document_sections.content: Most CRPS psychological-treatment studies are uncontrolled, use inadequately described or differing diagnostic criteria, and cannot establish efficacy under current IASP criteria. Table A1 summarizes the studies. In an RCT of 18 patients, home PT plus once-weekly autogenic relaxation for ten weeks and home PT alone improved pain, movement, and edema similarly; temperature improved significantly more with combined treatment (level 2), but the sample limited inference. In a paced-breathing pilot, healthy controls improved cardiac vagal tone, whereas CRPS patients did not despite comparable slowing of breathing; vagal tone was inversely associated with pain in CRPS (level 3). A sham-controlled crossover study found that a virtual limb flashing in time with the heartbeat, rather than out of time, significantly decreased pain and increased grip strength and cardiac vagal tone (level 2); clinical practicality is uncertain. Initial single-subject graded-exposure experiments in eight patients found significant parallel reductions in movement fear, pain, disability, and other symptoms (level 3). A later RCT found significantly greater improvements than pain-contingent usual care in pain, catastrophizing, perceived danger of activity, and disability at 6 month follow-up (level 2). Another RCT supported exposure in per-protocol but not intent-to-treat analyses (level 2); exposure to a wider variety of feared activities may improve its effects. Case reports describe pain reductions or resolution with biofeedback, relaxation, or imagery, but uncontrolled findings cannot establish efficacy or represent typical outcomes. An RCT of PT incorporating relaxation and cognitive work found significantly greater improvements in pain, active movement, and impairment than social-work control (level 2). In a pediatric RCT, once-weekly and three-times-weekly PT, both with six cognitive behavioral sessions, significantly improved pain and function against baseline; neither isolated psychological treatment effects (level 2). A 4week interdisciplinary program incorporating group psychotherapy improved function significantly without increased pain-related anxiety (level 3). In uncontrolled childhood series, a multidisciplinary program improved pain and function in 57% of 70 patients, while another reported symptom-free status in 92% of 103 patients; psychological counseling was given to 77% in the latter (level 3). In 49 adults, multidisciplinary care including biofeedback and cognitive behavioral therapy significantly improved mood, catastrophizing, coping, acceptance, and disability; improvement in pain approached significance (level 3). A series of 10 adults found reductions of 18% in sensory and 19% in motor/trophic symptoms after multidisciplinary care including cognitive-behavioral therapy and ACT (level 3). In other neuropathic pain, a high-quality RCT found cognitive behavioral analgesic benefit restricted to women (level 2), whereas meta-analysis of four controlled trials found no significant overall pain effect (level 1). CRPS-specific trials remain too few and small for firm conclusions, although available results support psychological care as a potentially useful component of interdisciplinary treatment.

document_sections.heading: Comparative Efficacy of Psychological Interventions in Other Non-CRPS Chronic Pain Disorders
document_sections.content: Meta-analyses in conditions other than CRPS found significant, at least moderate effects for progressive muscle relaxation and autogenic training (level 1), and significant effects for biofeedback in temporomandibular joint pain and migraine (level 1). Meta-analyses across psychological methods found significant benefit in several chronic pain conditions, including low back pain, fibromyalgia, rheumatoid arthritis, and cancer-related pain (level 1). A meta-analysis also supported cognitive behavioral interventions in children and adolescents with chronic pain (level 1). RCT findings generally indicate at least moderate improvements in pain, mood, and function across these conditions. Their relevance to CRPS is indirect, not proof of CRPS-specific efficacy.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Recommendations
document_sections.content: Few well-controlled CRPS-specific outcomes underpin psychological recommendations. Comprehensive education is recommended for all patients with acute or chronic CRPS, with early information for families about harms of disuse, reactivation, active self-management, and possible psychophysiological interactions. Such education might prevent distress and disuse that worsen disability or chronicity. For more persistent CRPS or inadequate response to limited care, the authors recommend individualized psychological assessment followed by focused psychological pain management.

document_sections.heading: Psychological Assessment
document_sections.content: Assessment should address comorbid Axis I or Axis II disorders, responses to CRPS, current stress, and significant others’ responses. Depression, anxiety, panic, and Posttraumatic Stress Disorder warrant attention; depression-related reductions in motivation and energy can impede active rehabilitation. Clinicians should also assess emotional arousal without diagnosable disorder. Pain-related fear and excessive avoidance merit particular assessment, while reasonable avoidance should not be mislabeled. Guarding and disuse can contribute to proximal myofascial pain that resembles CRPS spread. Fear of accidental contact may explain avoidance of crowds. Assessment should explore beliefs that CRPS inevitably worsens or spreads, that pain necessarily means tissue injury, that temporary treatment-related pain precludes later improvement, or that sympathetic blocks alone cure the condition. Patients should understand that CRPS pain does not signify tissue damage. An early focus on invasive procedures as a quick solution can undermine engagement in comprehensive rehabilitation; such procedures may nevertheless help some patients later. Research on CRPS internet discussions found that unrealistic expectations about medical outcomes are common.

document_sections.heading: Psychological Pain Management Interventions
document_sections.content: The authors recommend a treatment component incorporating relaxation, preferably with thermal or electromyographic biofeedback, and/or mindfulness-based stress reduction; cognitive pain-coping skills (CBT); approaches to living with persistent CRPS (ACT); and behavioral work on avoidance, disuse, and family responses. Additional targeted cognitive behavioral care may address identified stressors or psychiatric disorders. Relaxation and biofeedback aim to improve pain control and reduce emotional arousal and associated sympathetic activity. Evidence from non-CRPS pain supports several relaxation and mindfulness methods without establishing one as superior; patient preference, therapist preference, and daily home practice matter. Cognitive work should position the patient as an active participant, treat exacerbations as cues for self-management, and identify and modify catastrophic, fearful, or unrealistic beliefs. ACT may help maintain valued activities despite continuing symptoms. Reactivation should be incremental and realistically limited by pain, coordinated between psychologists and functional therapists to avoid both disuse and severe exacerbations. Experimental evidence offers some support for graded in vivo exposure to pain-related fear. Families should understand that appropriate reactivation can transiently increase pain, neither overprotect patients nor dismiss symptoms such as allodynia, and support constructive self-management. More than half of CRPS caregivers in one study experienced negative mood and significant strain associated with greater patient disability; causation could operate in either direction.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Psychological Considerations
document_sections.content: Psychological factors have not been convincingly shown to be necessary causes of chronic CRPS; they are often consequences, although plausible pathways could contribute in some patients. CRPS patients are not consistently shown to be psychologically distinct from other chronic pain patients. Once CRPS develops, emotional states may influence its pain more strongly than pain in other conditions. Evidence from other chronic pain conditions supports psychological methods, but adequate CRPS RCTs are lacking. Uncontrolled CRPS studies suggest potential usefulness of relaxation, biofeedback, mindfulness, cognitive and behavioral treatment, and graded exposure. Treatment should recognize learned disuse and integrate psychological care with the wider rehabilitation team.

document_sections.heading: Interventional Therapies
document_sections.content: Interventional approaches are numerous and generally inadequately studied. This review addresses sympathetic blocks, intravenous regional techniques, other blocks and infusions, neurolytic procedures, and implanted therapies. RCT evidence has recently advanced particularly for dorsal root ganglion stimulation, an advanced spinal cord stimulation approach for focal neuropathic pain. Traditional spinal cord stimulation is FDA-approved for chronic pain. The review incorporates topical reviews, meta-analyses, and Cochrane evidence. If conservative exercise does not produce meaningful functional improvement, more invasive care may be considered. Some clinics combine early nerve blocks with structured exercise; neuromodulation may be considered when substantial limitation or deterioration persists. Spinal cord and dorsal root ganglion stimulation may help a subset over the long term (level 2).

document_sections.heading: Sympathetic Nerve Blocks
document_sections.content: Local-anesthetic sympathetic blockade has a longstanding diagnostic and therapeutic role, originating partly from an earlier, now questioned view of CRPS as consistently driven by sympathetic overactivity. Autonomic manifestations include temperature and color asymmetry, inflammation, and edema. A subset with Sympathetically Maintained Pain (SMP) may have sympathetic–afferent coupling (level 4). Upper-limb blockade targets the level of Chassaignac’s tubercle at the sixth cervical vertebral body; lower-limb blockade targets the second and third lumbar vertebral body. Relief can outlast the anesthetic and sometimes persist (level 2; level 4). Other described sympatholytic methods include IV phentolamine, intravenous regional blocks with lidocaine, bretylium, clonidine, reserpine, or guanethidine, and epidural infusion. High-quality evidence does not establish a definitive therapeutic role for sympathetic nerve blocks. Their current use is largely empirical, but some patients might gain pain relief and a rehabilitative opportunity. A 2002 systematic review of literature from 1916 through 1999 concluded that blocks were not effective overall (level 1); heterogeneous older studies do not rule out responsive subsets (level 4), and less than 20% assessed block success critically. In a blinded crossover comparison involving seven patients, analgesia began within 30minutes with both local anesthetic and saline, but lasted significantly longer with local anesthetic: mean 3 d, 18h vs 19h (level 2). A comparison of stellate ganglion block and guanethidine intravenous regional block found significant improvement in both arms without a significant between-arm difference (level 3), but lacked a no-block control. In 20 patients, a blinded prospective study found closely correlated analgesic responses to sympathetic blockade and IV phentolamine (level 3). A study of 54 stellate ganglion blocks required 4 of 5 objective findings to define success; only 15 of 54 qualified (level 3). Horner’s syndrome or limb warming alone did not reliably demonstrate complete blockade. In another group of 33 patients with CRPS type I, even complete sympatholysis produced analgesia at a rate only a little higher than 50%. Some evidence supports stellate and lumbar blocks in selected patients (level 3); a short series alongside active physiotherapy is advocated by consensus (level 4). Evidence for lumbar blockade is especially limited. In a 9-patient study, adding botulinum toxin to bupivacaine increased mean analgesia duration from 10days to 71days (level 3).

document_sections.heading: Other Blocks and Infusion Techniques
document_sections.content: Case reports support brachial plexus blockade (level 4). Described indications for continuous infusion include peri-operative, post-trauma, and post-operative pain; vascular compromise; intractable CRPS I and II pain; and phantom-limb pain. Catheters have remained in place as long as three weeks and can deliver anesthetic, opioid, clonidine, or other adjuncts (level 4). Sympatholysis may last up to 2–3 weeks with 0.1 to 0.2% ropivacaine (level 4). In one severe CRPS II case 30days after carpal tunnel release, axillary bupivacaine at 0.1% and 2.5 mL/hour provided analgesia but dense motor and sensory blockade. Reduction within one day to 0.05%, cessation of basal infusion, and patient-controlled 1 mL every 15minutes maintained analgesia while allowing active PT; the catheter stayed for 1 week (level 4). Potential complications include bleeding, infection, intravascular or intrathecal injection, pneumothorax, and phrenic nerve paralysis. Epidural infusion permits titration of analgesia to preserve participation in PT; commonly described treatment combines clonidine and bupivacaine, with opioids added if necessary (level 4). Patient-controlled boluses may address fluctuations around exercise. In a blinded RCT of 26 patients, daily epidural clonidine 300 or 600mcg or placebo was administered for 3 consecutive days (level 2). The account also describes open-label treatment at a mean dose of 32mcg/hour for a mean of 32days and, separately, substantial relief with 300 and 700 microgram doses. It reports that 19 of 26 patients chose continued infusion averaging 43days at 3266 micrograms per hour; 17 of 19 improved significantly. These dose and duration accounts are inconsistent within the document. Adverse effects included dizziness, dry mouth, oral sores, and nausea; six of 19patients developed catheter infections and one developed meningitis. In a 14-patient open-label study, epidural bupivacaine-opioid infusion for an average of 4 days improved pain and movement in 13 of fourteen, with 11 of the 14 described as having CRPS resolution at trial end (level 3). Another 26-patient study combined 0.25% cervical epidural bupivacaine for seven days with PT: 83% reported pain improvement, 63% considered their condition acceptable, and only 8% became completely pain-free (level 3). Epidural-catheter infection rates in CRPS have been reported as high as 31%. For prolonged use, surgical sterility, subcutaneous tunneling away from the spinal entry site, and weekly dressing changes are recommended (level 4). Back pain, sensorimotor loss, and bowel or bladder dysfunction suggest epidural abscess; fever, neck pain, or photophobia may precede them. In a separate catheter study, 19 out of 350 patients developed infection; all received antibiotics and catheter removal, with none requiring surgery. Intrathecal bupivacaine initially relieved pain in a series of three refractory patients, but CRPS progressed in all (level 4). Intrathecal baclofen produced analgesia and functional improvement in n =7 patients with severe dystonia (level 3 evidence); its original investigators later stopped using the infusion because of adverse effects. Evidence for intrathecal infusion without dystonia is limited. Epidural infusion is sometimes adopted after intermittent blocks, but infection risk requires further prospective study.

document_sections.heading: Neurolytic Sympathetic Procedures
document_sections.content: Surgical sympathectomy has historically treated SMP and other sympathetic conditions since 1889. Endoscopic and radiofrequency methods have also been described (level 3). A literature review found initial surgical failure up to 35%, often attributed to patient selection (level 1); incorrect diagnosis, insufficient resection, reinnervation, and contralateral innervation are other proposed explanations (level 4). There is no high-quality support for ablative sympathectomy in CRPS. Its use has declined because substantial adverse effects outweigh uncertain efficacy (level 4). Previous symptoms or post-sympathectomy neuralgia can emerge 6 months to two years later; neuralgia incidence reached 44% in one open-surgery causalgia series. Re-resection or spinal cord stimulation has been proposed for this neuralgia without conclusive evidence. In over 350 radiofrequency procedures for hyperhidrosis rather than CRPS, 86% showed sustained sympathetic interruption at three-year follow-up; pain and function were not assessed (level 3). A non-peer-reviewed report described post-procedure neuralgia around 5% (level 4). RCT data on pulsed radiofrequency sympathetic procedures for CRPS are unavailable. Neurodestructive methods are rarely recommended for chronic pain because they can worsen pain or cause deafferentation or neuralgia; alcohol or phenol neurolysis is now largely confined to terminal illness. Radiofrequency permits better lesion-size control than neurolysis (level 4), but its role remains uncertain.

document_sections.heading: Neurostimulation
document_sections.content: The 1965 Melzack and Wall gate theory supplied an early proposed mechanism for spinal cord stimulation, involving preferential activation of large afferents and inhibition of smaller C and A-delta fibers. A search covering 2000 to 2021 identified 118 CRPS-and-SCS publications, including eight RCTs and three meta-analyses; Table A2 summarizes studies. After failure of functional restoration and intensive noninvasive care, spinal cord stimulation or dorsal root ganglion stimulation may be considered. Conventional SCS acts at the spinal dorsal column, whereas DRG stimulation targets pathways at the dorsal root. Reported benefits after failed conservative care include reduced pain and opioid use and improved function and quality of life. In Kemler et al.’s randomized study of CRPS type I lasting 6 months or longer, 36 patients were allocated SCS plus an inadequately specified PT program and 18 PT alone (level 2). Successful trials led to implantation in 24 of 36 assigned SCS. At 6-month follow-up, SCS improved pain and perceived overall change but not clinically meaningful function; modest significant benefits were partly sustained for two years. Cervical and lumbar SCS did not differ in effectiveness or complication rates in a subsequent analysis. In Kriek et al.’s randomized waveform study, Thirteen patients supplied skin-blister samples; the protocol included a two week trial at 40Hz, then 3 months at 40Hz after implantation, followed by assessment of 40Hz, 500Hz, 1200Hz, burst, and placebo settings and another 3 months using preferred settings (level 2). Findings suggested reduced T-cell activity and IP-10 over time; reduced vascular endothelial growth factor and platelet derived growth factor were attributed tentatively to greater tissue oxygenation. In van Eijs et al.’s randomized study of 36 patients, Twenty-four proceeded to implantation; after 1 year, 20 out of 24 (83%) retained significant pain reduction. Brush-evoked allodynia may predict poorer SCS response (level 2). The ACCURATE randomized comparison assigned lower-limb CRPS type 1 or 2 patients to DRG stimulation or SCS in a 1:1 ratio (level 2). Eligibility required a six-month pain history and Budapest Criteria diagnosis. Trials lasted 3 days to 30days; mean duration was 5.8 days (SD 2.8days) for DRG and 5.8 days (SD 5.1days) for SCS. Implantation required at least 50% VAS pain reduction without new neurological complaints. At 12 months, treatment success was 81.2% with DRG versus 56.7% with SCS; suggested quality-of-life and psychological advantages were hypothetical. A retrospective analysis of 61 DRG recipients assessed outcomes at 1, 3, 6, 9, and 12month follow-ups; paresthesia-free relief rose from 16.4% at 1 month to 38.3% at 12months (level 3). Its authors concluded that paresthesia is not necessary for relief. Dworkin et al. characterized SCS recommendations as weak, urged shared decisions about benefits, risks, and alternatives, and suggested reserving it for inadequate response to noninvasive treatment and sympathetic blocks or when blocks are inappropriate. A 2020 pooled analysis identified 217 patients with permanent DRG implantation at 12months: weighted mean pain was 3.4 on a 10 point NRS, 63% achieved 50% pain relief, and mean NRS reductions were 4.9 for CRPS type 1, 4.6 for causalgia, and 3.9 for low back pain (level 1). Supporting evidence for SCS and DRG exists, but further corroboration and high-quality research are needed.

document_sections.heading: IV Regional Anesthetic Blocks (IVRA)
document_sections.content: IVRA delivers drugs to a tourniqueted affected limb. Reported agents include guanethidine, lidocaine, bretylium, clonidine, droperidol, ketanserin, and reserpine. A meta-analysis selected 11 sympathetic-suppressor trials, including 9 IVRA studies and 6 involving guanethidine; its pooled findings did not establish an effect for IVRA overall or guanethidine IVRA specifically (level 1), although responsive subsets remain possible. In a blinded crossover trial of 60 CRPS I patients receiving four blocks at four-day intervals, initial response favored the 0.5% lidocaine control; at six months after the final block, 35% had significant relief without a guanethidine–control difference (level 2). Because the control involved anesthetic and a tourniquet, it may itself have been active. An enriched crossover study found no difference between guanethidine and placebo and ended early owing to adverse effects (level 2). A 21-patient crossover study found no discernible short-term differences between guanethidine, reserpine, and saline (level 3); a tourniquet effect complicates interpretation. Another small comparison found relief but no differences between reserpine, guanethidine, and lidocaine (level 3). A randomized comparison favoring bretylium over lidocaine was an exception (level 2). A comparison of guanethidine IVRA and stellate ganglion blockade in 19 patients reported comparable effects. Overall IVRA efficacy evidence is low quality; bretylium, phentolamine, clonidine, lidocaine, and ketorolac lack high-quality supporting evidence in this setting. Bretylium is unavailable in the USA.

document_sections.heading: Other IV Infusions
document_sections.content: IV phentolamine has been proposed to identify SMP. In Arner’s uncontrolled study, approximately 50% of adults with causalgia or RSD responded analgesically, with a strong relationship to later guanethidine response. Among children, 37 of the 47 responded markedly to phentolamine and 32/37 had an excellent subsequent guanethidine response (level 3). The absence of a control limits these findings. A separate prospective study found no significant differences among placebo, phentolamine, and phenylephrine for pain, QST testing, blood flow, or hyperalgesia (level 3). A randomized blinded study of 16 CRPS I or II patients compared lidocaine infusions at 1, 2, and 3mcg/mL with placebo. Lidocaine reduced cold-evoked pain and cold or touch allodynia; spontaneous pain decreased only at the highest serum level. Punctate-evoked pain did not change (level 2 evidence for short-term benefit). IV phentolamine has mainly served to distinguish SMP from SIP, and both phentolamine and lidocaine infusions have fallen out of clinical favor. Figure 4 depicts a consensus-based empirical sequence from minimally invasive blocks through catheter infusions and neurostimulation to surgical or experimental treatments.

document_sections.heading: Motor Cortex Stimulation
document_sections.content: Motor cortex stimulation is described as the most invasive option discussed for CRPS pain. Its proposed mechanism is modulation of abnormal activity in thalamic relay nuclei; normalization of lost inhibitory control has been described to a greater extent than with somatosensory cortex stimulation (level 4). A trial precedes implantation, and complications may resemble those of other chronic neurosurgical implants, although reported risks are uncommon (level 4). Consistent with the Malibu scheme, simpler, safer, less invasive, and less costly approaches should precede experimental invasive methods. Inadequate or partial response may justify stepwise progression while noninterventional treatment continues. The authors find advances in diagnosis, outcome measures, and evidence-based treatment in this 5th edition, but few CRPS interventions have convincing efficacy evidence. Interdisciplinary management remains necessary; evaluating treatment effects within empirically identified subtypes may eventually improve targeting. Every intervention requires continuing assessment of its risks, benefits, and costs.

document_sections.heading: Appendix
document_sections.content: Table A1 summarizes psychological and behavioral intervention studies in publication order, including their designs, populations, interventions, and outcomes. It identifies improvements in several uncontrolled reports and selected randomized comparisons, while also showing differing results across interventions. Both Oerlemans et al. reports used the same sample. Table A2 summarizes SCS and DRG studies by author, design, sample, and outcome, including pain relief, patient satisfaction, complications-related findings, and comparative stimulation results. Its ACCURATE trial entry reports treatment success with >50% pain relief at 3months as 81.2% for DRG and 55.7% for SCS; the narrative elsewhere gives 81.2% and 56.7% at 12 months, respectively. The tables do not resolve this difference in SCS percentages and timepoints.
